title: Honduran Illegal Alien Indicted for Attempted Coercion and Enticement of A Minor and Illegal Reentry of A Removed Alien
body: Press Release Honduran Illegal Alien Indicted for Attempted Coercion and Enticement of A Minor and Illegal Reentry of A Removed Alien Monday, October 26, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Eastern District of Louisiana shane.jones@usdoj.gov NEW ORLEANS – LESLI JOEL CALIX-SARMIENTO (“CALIX-SARMIENTO”) , age 36, a Honduran national, was charged in a two-count indictment on October 23, 2026, with attempted coercion and enticement of a minor, in violation of Title 18, United States Code, Section 2422(b), and illegal reentry of a removed alien, in violation of Title 8, United States Code, Section 1326(a), announced U.S. Attorney David I. Courcelle. According to Count 1 of the indictment, between August 27, 2026, and August 28, 2026, CALIX-SARMIENTO persuaded and enticed an individual he believed to be a fifteen-year-old female to engage in illegal and illicit sexual activity. In addition, on or about August 28, 2026, CALIX-SARMIENTO , an alien, was found in the United States after having been deported and removed therefrom on or about August 27, 2013, February 11, 2014, and March 11, 2014, without the approval of the Attorney General of the United States, or his designated successor, the Secretary of the Department of Homeland Security, having expressly consented to the defendant’s reapplication for admission into the United States. Through a partnership between state and federal authorities, the U.S. Attorney’s Office adopted the state charges, and is now federally prosecuting CALIX-SARMIENTO . If convicted of Count 1, CALIX-SARMIENTO faces a mandatory minimum of ten (10) years and up to a lifetime in prison, at least five (5) years and up to a lifetime of supervised release, as well as  sex offender registration. If convicted of  Count 2, CALIX-SARMIENTO faces up to two (2) years imprisonment, and up to one (1) year of supervised release.  As to each count, CALIX-SARMIENTO also faces up to a $250,000 fine and a $100 mandatory special assessment fee. U. S. Attorney Courcelle reiterated that the indictment is merely a charge and that the guilt of the defendant must be proven beyond a reasonable doubt. U.S. Attorney Courcelle praised the work of the Homeland Security Investigations, Louisiana Internet Crimes Against Children (ICAC) Task Force and the Assumption Parish Sheriff’s Department in investigating this matter. Assistant United States Attorney Mary Anne Flippo of the Public Integrity Unit and Human Trafficking and Child Exploitation Task Force is in charge of the prosecution. This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by United States Attorneys’ Offices and the Criminal Division's Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section (CEOS), Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state and local resources to better locate, apprehend and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the Internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit www.projectsafechildhood.gov . *     *    * Contact Shane M. title: Lake Charles Man with Previous Child Pornography Conviction Sentenced to More than 33 Years in Federal Prison for Conspiracy to Distribute Child Pornography
body: Press Release Lake Charles Man with Previous Child Pornography Conviction Sentenced to More than 33 Years in Federal Prison for Conspiracy to Distribute Child Pornography Monday, October 26, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Western District of Louisiana LAKE CHARLES – On October 15, 2026, United States District Judge James D. Cain Jr. sentenced Sean Alexander Meeks , 49, of Lake Charles, to 400 months (33.4 years) in federal prison for Conspiracy to Distribute Child Pornography, followed by 15 years of supervised release.  Meeks previously pled guilty on May 20, 2026. “Federal criminal law rightly punishes recidivist child sex predators severely, and Judge Cain’s 400-month sentence of Sean Meeks shows the consequences when these predators choose to continue engaging in this heinous criminal conduct,” said U.S. Attorney Zachary A. Keller. “Our Office works alongside our federal, state, and local law enforcement partners every day to investigate and prosecute these crimes, and we will continue prioritizing cases involving recidivists like Mr. Meeks and seeking severe penalties when we bring defendants like him into court.” “This 400-month sentence sends a clear message: those who exploit children will be identified, investigated, and held accountable for their actions. This defendant’s prior conviction and continued criminal conduct demonstrates the serious threat posed by repeat offenders,” said Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) New Orleans Special Agent in Charge Matt Wright. “HSI Lake Charles is proud to work alongside the Montgomery County Constable’s Office, the Montgomery County District Attorney’s Office Internet Crimes Against Children (ICAC) Unit, the Calcasieu Parish Sheriff’s Office, and other ICAC partners to bring predators like Meeks to justice.” According to court documents, investigators with the Montgomery County Sheriff’s Office in Texas (MCSO) identified Meeks as the administrator of an online messaging group where illegal child sexual content was being exchanged. Undercover detectives working online observed Meeks directing the group’s activities, communicating with chatroom members, and distributing illicit material. Law enforcement was able to trace the online account activity to Meeks, who was residing in Lake Charles as this conduct occurred. After law enforcement arrested Meeks on April 17, 2025, investigators conducted a forensic analysis of his smartphone and were able to verify his connection to the online group. In particular, his device contained the same online accounts observed by investigators and also contained 17 videos and two images depicting child sexual abuse that had appeared in the same form as in the chat room. The investigation further uncovered Meeks’s prior conviction for possession of child pornography in Vernon Parish in 2007. U.S. Attorney Zachary A. Keller for the Western District of Louisiana made the announcement. HSI, MCSO, Montgomery County District Attorney’s Office Internet Crimes Against Children (ICAC) Unit, and the Calcasieu Parish Sheriff’s Office investigated this case. It was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Daniel Vermaelen, with assistance from Legal Assistant Kimberly Blanchard. This case was prosecuted as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice.  Led by the U.S. Attorneys' Offices and the Criminal Division's Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section (CEOS), Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state and local resources to better locate, apprehend and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the Internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. Learn more at https://www.justice.gov/psc/about-project-safe-childhood . You may find a copy of this press release (and any updates) on the website of the United States Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Louisiana at www.justice.gov/usao-wdla. Related court documents and information may be found on the website of the District Court for the Western District of Louisiana at www.lawd.uscourts.gov or at https://www.lawd.uscourts.gov/cmecf-pacer, under Case Number 2:25-cr-280. ### CONTACT: Public Affairs: Cara.Alexander@usdoj.gov www.justice.gov/usao-wdla (337) 262-6704 Updated October 26, 2026 Topic Project Safe Childhood Component USAO - Louisiana, Western

title: Oswego Man Charged with Sexual Exploitation of a Child and Transportation and Possession of Child Pornography
body: Press Release Oswego Man Charged with Sexual Exploitation of a Child and Transportation and Possession of Child Pornography Monday, October 26, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Northern District of New York USANYN-MediaInquiry@usa.doj.gov On October 9, 2026, Emerardo Abisai Vasquez-Lopez, age 20, of Oswego, New York, appeared in federal court in Syracuse, New York, before United States Magistrate Judge Mitchell J. Katz on charges related to his alleged sexual exploitation of a child and his transportation and possession of child pornography. Vasquez-Lopez was ordered detained pending further proceedings. First Assistant United States Attorney John A. Sarcone III and Anthony Patrone, Acting Special Agent in Charge of the Buffalo Field Office of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), made the announcement. The complaint filed against Vasquez-Lopez alleges that between August and October of 2024, Vasquez-Lopez sexually abused a 9-year-old child and created images and videos of that abuse. Following the abuse, Vasquez-Lopez uploaded the material he created to a cloud storage account under his control. Vasquez-Lopez also downloaded child pornography from the same cloud storage account and possessed some of that material on an electronic device belonging to him that was seized at the time of his arrest. First Assistant U.S. Attorney Sarcone stated, “This defendant’s abuse of a vulnerable child coupled with his creation of images and videos memorializing that abuse is absolutely reprehensible. The swift actions taken by HSI and the New York State Police to find and detain the defendant has ensured that while these charges are pending, he will be behind bars and cannot pray on children and endanger our community.” “Sexual abuse and the creation and sharing of child sexual abuse material inflict profound and lasting harm on children, their families and the communities that depend on adults to protect them,” said Acting Special Agent in Charge Anthony Patrone of HSI Buffalo. “These alleged acts betray the trust and safety every child deserves, while the continued circulation of such material extends the victimization and endangers the public. HSI Syracuse works every day with our law enforcement partners to identify those who target and exploit vulnerable children, safeguard victims and hold offenders accountable." The sexual exploitation charge filed against Vasquez-Lopez carries a term of 15 to 30 years in federal prison. The transportation charge carries a term of five to 20 years in federal prison. The possession charge carries a term of up to 20 years in federal prison. Each count carries a fine of up to $250,000 and a term of supervised release of at least 5 years and up to life.  If convicted, Vasquez-Lopez will also be required to register as a sex offender upon his release from prison and may ultimately be deported and removed from the United States based on his lack of lawful status. A defendant’s sentence is imposed by a judge based on the particular statutes the defendant is convicted of violating, the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other factors. The charges in the complaint are merely accusations. The defendant is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty. HSI and the New York State Police are investigating the case. The case is being prosecuted by Adrian LaRochelle as part of Project Safe Childhood. Project Safe Childhood is a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse. Led by the U.S. Attorneys’ Offices and the Criminal Division’s Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section (CEOS), Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state and local resources to better locate, apprehend and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the Internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. title: Federal agents arrest former CEO of child & adolescent residential treatment center on federal child pornography, coercion charges
body: Press Release Federal agents arrest former CEO of child & adolescent residential treatment center on federal child pornography, coercion charges Monday, October 26, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Southern District of Ohio COLUMBUS, Ohio – The former CEO of a Belmont County residential treatment facility for children and adolescents was arrested by federal agents on child pornography and coercion charges. Randall J. MacKendrick, 59, of St. Clairsville, was arrested in August on local charges after attempting to meet up with who he believed was a teenage girl. One month later, while out on bond, MacKendrick was re-arrested for being in contact with a minor female who was a former patient at the treatment center. In October, the FBI learned MacKendrick is a suspect in a May kidnapping and rape of a 14-year-old female in Perry County. MacKendrick served as the CEO of Fox Run Center for Children and Adolescents in St. Clairsville. The facility treats boys ages 5 to 12 and girls ages 12 to 17. He appeared in federal court in Columbus this afternoon for an initial appearance, and his federal charges were unsealed at that time. According to the charging documents, in June 2026, MacKendrick began communicating online with a North Ridgeville police officer acting undercover and posing as a 14-year-old female. MacKendrick allegedly communicated with who he believed was a teenage girl until August 2026, sending the undercover officer sexually explicit messages, offering to send gifts and requesting to meet in person. It is alleged that MacKendrick traveled to central Ohio in July 2026 attempting to meet up with the fictitious teenager at Polaris Fashion Place, Tanger Outlets and a Holiday Inn. In August, MacKendrick allegedly traveled to South Central Park in Lorain County to meet up with the purported teenager. MacKendrick was arrested on local charges after departing the park. In his vehicle, law enforcement found multiple sex toys, several condoms and three cell phones. Also in August, Belmont County Sheriff’s Office detectives searched MacKendrick’s office and residence. During their forensic analysis of MacKendrick’s digital devices, deputies discovered images and videos of child sexual abuse material. MacKendrick was released on bond in his local case but was re-arrested in September, when law enforcement officers learned MacKendrick was allegedly in contact with a former patient of Fox Run who is 17 years old. MacKendrick’s bond was increased and he was released again. In October, FBI agents learned MacKendrick is a suspect in a Perry County case involving the kidnapping and rape of a 14-year-old. MacKendrick’s DNA matches DNA recovered from the victim. That investigation is still ongoing. MacKendrick was arrested Saturday in West Virginia and transferred to the Southern District of Ohio prior to today’s initial appearance. The defendant is charged with possessing child pornography, a federal crime punishable by up to 20 years in prison, and attempted coercion and enticement of a minor, which carries a potential penalty of at least 10 years and up to life in prison. Dominick S. Gerace II, United States Attorney for the Southern District of Ohio; Jason Cromartie, Special Agent in Charge, Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Cincinnati Division; the North Ridgeville Police Department; and Belmont County Sheriff James G. Zusack announced the charges. Assistant United States Attorneys Emily Czerniejewski and Tyler J. Aagard are representing the United States in this case. A criminal complaint merely contains allegations, and defendants are presumed innocent unless proven guilty in a court of law. This case is part of Project Safe Childhood , a nationwide initiative launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse. title: New York Woman Charged With $1.1M Check Cashing Scheme
body: Press Release New York Woman Charged With $1.1M Check Cashing Scheme Monday, October 26, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release Office of Public Affairs Xue Fang Cheng, 55, of New York, was arrested today after a federal grand jury in the Eastern District of New York returned an indictment on Oct. 23 charging Cheng with providing illegal check cashing services. According to court documents, Cheng was an owner of a New York convenience store that provided unlicensed check cashing services to at least three individuals, including a social adult day care center owner and an undercover law enforcement agent. Cheng directed that checks be deposited in business bank accounts held by various companies and controlled by others, and she provided cash to her customers for a 2–3% fee. Cheng documented the cashed checks via text and audio messages and instructed the undercover agent that they should “plan to do [it] long term,” cautioning that “[i]t is very dangerous.” From March 2025 through July 2026, Cheng allegedly participated in providing over $1.1 million in cash to her customers. In connection with the investigation, law enforcement seized approximately $875,000. Cheng is charged with conspiracy to operate an unlicensed money transmitting business. If convicted, she faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison. Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division; U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella, Jr. for the Eastern District of New York; Acting Deputy Inspector General for Investigations Miranda L. Bennett of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General (HHS-OIG); Pete Gizas, Acting Special Agent in Charge, Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) New York; and Jessica S. Tisch, Commissioner, New York City Police Department (NYPD), made the announcement. HHS-OIG, HSI New York, and the NYPD are investigating the case. Deputy Chief Patrick J. Campbell and Trial Attorney Leonid Sandlar of the Fraud Division’s Health Care Fraud Section are prosecuting the case. On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the Fraud Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs. The Department of Justice’s Health Care Fraud Strike Force Program, currently comprised of nine strike forces operating in federal districts across the country, has charged more than 6,200 defendants who collectively billed federal health care programs and private insurers more than $45 billion since 2007. In addition, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, working in conjunction with the Office of the Inspector General for the Department of Health and Human Services, are taking steps to hold providers accountable for their involvement in health care fraud schemes. More information can be found at www.justice.gov/criminal-fraud/health-care-fraud-unit . An indictment is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law. Updated October 26, 2026 Topic Fraud Component National Fraud Enforcement Division Press Release Number: 26-1261

title: Public Company Officers Plead Guilty to International Securities Fraud Conspiracies
body: Press Release Public Company Officers Plead Guilty to International Securities Fraud Conspiracies Monday, October 26, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Northern District of Georgia ATLANTA – Zoltan Nagy, a Canadian businessman, and Glenn Laken, an Illinois trader previously convicted of federal securities fraud and racketeering offenses, have pleaded guilty to conspiring to commit securities fraud in connection with international pump-and-dump schemes that resulted in over $1 million in losses. Three Canadian co-conspirators, Phillip Sewell, Richard Tang, and Davies Wong, previously pleaded guilty to similar charges. “These defendants engaged in sophisticated stock price manipulation that harmed investors and undermined confidence in the market,” said U.S. Attorney Theodore S. Hertzberg. “With the assistance of our partners in law enforcement and at the Securities and Exchange Commission, we will continue to aggressively root out and prosecute criminals who perpetrate securities fraud.” “These defendants manipulated the stock market for their own financial gain, exploiting investors and compromising the security of brokerage accounts to carry out their schemes,” said Marlo Graham, Special Agent in Charge of FBI Atlanta. “These guilty pleas underscore the FBI’s commitment to working with our law enforcement partners to investigate complex financial crimes, hold those responsible accountable, and protect the integrity of our financial markets.” According to U.S. Attorney Hertzberg, the indictment, and other information presented in court: Nagy and Laken were the majority shareholders of two different publicly traded penny stock companies at the heart of separate, but substantially similar, pump-and-dump schemes. Both schemes involved hacking U.S.-based online consumer brokerage accounts and forcing purchases of worthless penny stocks that Nagy’s and Laken’s co-conspirators controlled. The Lotus Scheme Nagy was the sole officer and director of Lotus Bio-Technology Development Corp. (“Lotus”), a penny stock company that traded publicly under the ticker LBTD. By the beginning of August 2017, Nagy, Tang, Wong, and Sewell controlled the vast bulk of outstanding LBTD shares that were available for public trading. On August 16, 2017, Rahim Mohamed, another co-conspirator, or someone acting at his direction, allegedly hacked into a U.S.-based online brokerage account and forced it to purchase 200,000 LBTD shares. At almost the same time, Wong and other co-conspirators sold approximately 261,000 LBTD shares, the majority of which were ultimately purchased by the hacked brokerage account at inflated prices. On September 19, 2017, the co-conspirators struck again, on a significantly larger scale. Mohamed, or others acting at his direction, allegedly hacked into 24 customer accounts at multiple U.S.-based online brokerage firms and forced them to purchase millions of LBTD shares. While the compromised accounts were forced to buy LBTD shares, Wong and other co-conspirators sold approximately 7.75 million LBTD shares for nearly $1.1 million in proceeds. In the weeks that followed, the proceeds from these sales were divided between Nagy, Wong, Tang, Mohamed, Sewell, and others. The Good Gaming Scheme Laken was the CEO, chairman, and controlling shareholder of a publicly traded company that, by late 2017, owned 61% of Good Gaming, Inc., a penny stock company that traded publicly under the ticker GMER. In 2002, Laken was convicted of racketeering conspiracy, wire fraud, and other federal charges related to a pension fund fraud and conspiracy to commit securities and wire fraud related to a stock manipulation scheme. Between January 12 and January 18, 2018, Tang coordinated with Laken to transfer approximately 2.9 million GMER shares to accounts held by co-conspirators. On January 22, 2018, Mohamed, or others acting at his direction, allegedly hacked into several accounts at U.S.-based online brokerage firms and forced them to purchase more than one million GMER shares. At the same time, other co-conspirators sold more than 700,000 of the GMER shares they had originally obtained from Laken for nearly $170,000. The proceeds were then divided between Laken, Tang, Mohamed, and other co-conspirators. On October 20, 2026, Zoltan Nagy, 60, of Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit securities fraud. His sentencing hearing is set for January 20, 2027, at 2:00 p.m. before U.S. District Judge Victoria M. Calvert. On September 25, 2026, Glenn Laken, 72, of Chicago, Illinois, pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit securities fraud. His sentencing hearing is set for January 13, 2027, at 11:00 a.m. Sewell, Tang, and Wong previously pleaded guilty for their involvement in the Lotus Scheme: On September 17, 2024, Phillip Sewell, 65, of Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit securities fraud. His sentencing hearing is set for January 22, 2027, at 10:30 a.m. On October 23, 2024, Richard Tang, 49, of Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit wire fraud. His sentencing hearing is set for January 21, 2027, at 10:30 a.m. On November 29, 2023, Davies Wong, 67, of Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit securities fraud. His sentencing hearing is set for January 21, 2027, at 1:30 p.m. Tang faces up to twenty years’ imprisonment, and Laken, Nagy, Sewell, and Wong face up to five years’ imprisonment. Each defendant also may be ordered to pay restitution to the victims and a fine of up to $250,000 or twice the gain or loss amount, whichever is greater. In determining the actual sentence, the Court will consider the United States Sentencing Guidelines, which are not binding but provide appropriate sentencing ranges for most offenders. Rahim Mohamed, 50, of Calgary, Alberta, Canada is still at large. Information regarding his whereabouts should be reported to local law enforcement. This case is being investigated by the Federal Bureau of Investigation with substantial assistance from the Securities and Exchange Commission. Assistant United States Attorneys Benjamin Wylly, Adam Sunstrom, and Samir Kaushal are prosecuting the case. First Assistant United States Attorney Nathan P. Kitchens and former Assistant United States Attorneys Tal C. Chaiken, Alex R. Sistla, and Christopher J. Huber previously prosecuted the case. For further information please contact the U.S. Attorney’s Public Affairs Office at USAGAN.PressEmails@usdoj.gov or (404) 581-6185. The Internet address for the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Georgia is http://www.justice.gov/usao-ndga . title: Tioga County Man Sentenced to 15 Years in Federal Prison for Sexual Exploitation of a Child and Transportation of Child Pornography
body: Press Release Tioga County Man Sentenced to 15 Years in Federal Prison for Sexual Exploitation of a Child and Transportation of Child Pornography Monday, October 26, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Northern District of New York USANYN-MediaInquiry@usa.doj.gov Tristan Kovacs, age 23, of Waverly, New York, was sentenced today to 15 years in federal prison for sexual exploitation a child and transportation of child pornography announced First Assistant United States Attorney John A. Sarcone III and Craig L. Tremaroli, Special Agent in Charge of the Albany Field Office of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI). In addition to the term of imprisonment imposed, U.S. District Judge, Anthony J. Brindisi, also imposed a 15-year term of supervision which will begin after Kovacs is released from prison at which time Kovacs will also be required to register as a sex offender. As part of his guilty plea in the case, Kovacs previously admitted that in April of 2025, he photographed himself engaging in sexually explicit conduct with a 10-year-old female child which he then uploaded to a pornographic website so others could view and download the image. First Assistant United States Attorney John A. Sarcone III stated: “The defendant’s conduct in this case, which included his victimization of a vulnerable 10-year-old child, is abhorrent and the significant sentence imposed is just punishment for that level of depravity. Over the next three decades, the defendant will either be incarcerated or under strict supervision which will help to ensure that he is never again in a position to harm another child.” “While Mr. Kovacs spends the next 15 years behind bars in federal prison, the FBI’s Child Exploitation and Human Trafficking Task Force will continue to relentlessly investigate and hold accountable any other sick predators like him who seek to exploit our children," said Craig Tremaroli, Special Agent in Charge of the Federal Bureau of Investigation's Albany Field Office. "The victims in these cases deserve swift justice, and this FBI stands ready to deliver that to them so they can focus on rebuilding their lives.” This case was investigated by the FBI’s Albany Division Child Exploitation and Human Trafficking Task Force and the New York State Police with assistance from the Waverly New York Police Department and the Broome County Sheriff’s Office. Assistant U.S. Attorney Adrian S. LaRochelle prosecuted the case as part of Project Safe Childhood. Project Safe Childhood is a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse. Led by the U.S. Attorneys' Offices and the Criminal Division's Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section (CEOS), Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state and local resources to better locate, apprehend and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the Internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. title: DC Man Pleads Guilty to Escaping from Baltimore Correctional Facility
body: Press Release DC Man Pleads Guilty to Escaping from Baltimore Correctional Facility Monday, October 26, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Maryland Baltimore, Maryland – A Washington, DC man pled guilty in federal court, today, to charges stemming from his escape from a Baltimore correctional facility. Lamont Antwan Warren, 46, pled guilty to escape from custody. Kelly O. Hayes, U.S. Attorney for the District of Maryland, announced the guilty plea with Clinton J. Fuchs, U.S. Marshal for the District of Maryland (USMS). According to his guilty plea, in May 2025, while serving a five-year sentence for sex-abuse crimes, Warren escaped from a Baltimore Volunteer of America’s Residential Re-Entry Center (RRC). On May 22, authorities transferred Warren from a Waymart, Pennsylvania correctional facility to Baltimore to serve the remainder of his sentence in community housing. Additionally, due to relocating, Warren was required to register as a sex offender in Maryland within three days of his arrival. One day after his transfer, RRC staff found Warren under the influence of an unknown drug. Law enforcement searched Warren and discovered unknown narcotics in his possession. RRC staff then attempted to require Warren to meet with his case worker. But instead, Warren ignored directives, refused to meet with his case worker, and then exited the facility. Two minutes later, RRC staff received an alert that Warren tampered with his GPS monitor. Staff then discovered the device in the RRC’s parking lot. Before Warren escaped, he did not register as a sex offender. Then on June 25, 2025, authorities found and apprehended Warren in Washington, DC. If convicted, Warren faces a maximum sentence of five years in prison for escape from custody. Actual sentences for federal crimes are typically less than the maximum penalties. A federal district court judge determines sentencing after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors. U.S. Attorney Hayes commended USMS for its work in the investigation. Ms. Hayes also thanked Assistant U.S. Attorney Alexandria A. Bell who is prosecuting the federal case. For more information about the Maryland U.S. Attorney’s Office, its priorities, and resources available to help the community, visit justice.gov/usao-md . # # # Contact Kevin Nash USAMD.Press@usdoj.gov 410-209-4946 Updated October 26, 2026 Components USAO - Maryland U.S. Marshals Service

title: Soldier pretends to be a woman to get minors to produce child pornography
body: Press Release Soldier pretends to be a woman to get minors to produce child pornography Monday, October 26, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Kansas TOPEKA, KAN. – A U.S. Army Soldier stationed in Kansas was sentenced to 40 years in prison for coaxing minors into producing child sexual abuse material (CSAM). According to court documents, Bebak Gurung, 22, of Fort Riley pleaded guilty to two counts of sexual exploitation of a minor- production of child pornography. In 2025, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) received information that a minor in New York had been victimized through various online messaging platforms and provided with saved communications between the victim and the perpetrator as evidence. During an investigation, FBI agents determined that Gurung had instructed the minor to produce videos while engaged in sexually explicit conduct. At the time Gurung was stationed at Fort Riley and agents determined he was on the installation while communicating with the victim. While executing a search warrant in the barracks, agents seized several of Gurung’s electronic devices where they found CSAM and evidence that led to the discovery of another minor victim in Kansas. “Mr. Gurung lied to his to victims about being a female to more easily gain their trust, which is why we must teach our children that not everyone is who they say they are, particularly online,” said U.S. Attorney Ryan A. Kriegshauser. “Fortunately, parents were willing to report this crime to the proper authorities so that his actions could be exposed and ultimately stopped.” "Protecting children from online predators remains a priority for the FBI. Those who exploit our children for sexual gratification will be identified, investigated, and held accountable for their actions,” said FBI Kansas City Special Agent in Charge Chris Ormerod. “The FBI, alongside our law enforcement partners will not stop in pursuing these offenders, to ensure our most vulnerable are protected from those who prey on them and are brought to justice.” The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) investigated the case. Assistant U.S. Attorney Sara Walton prosecuted the case. Project Safe Childhood This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by U.S. Attorneys’ Offices and CEOS, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to better locate, apprehend, and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the Internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit https://www.justice.gov/psc . ### Updated October 26, 2026 Topic Project Safe Childhood Component USAO - Kansas

title: Scotia Man Pleads Guity to Attempted Coercion and Enticement of a Minor and Possession of Child Pornography
body: Press Release Scotia Man Pleads Guity to Attempted Coercion and Enticement of a Minor and Possession of Child Pornography Monday, October 26, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Northern District of New York USANYN-MediaInquiry@usa.doj.gov On October 19, 2026, Zachary Long, age 27, of Scotia, New York, pled guilty before United States District Judge Mae A. D’Agostino to attempted online coercion and enticement of a minor and possession of child pornography. First Assistant United States Attorney John A. Sarcone III and Craig L. Tremaroli, Special Agent in Charge of the Albany Field Office of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), made the announcement. During his plea, Long admitted that between August 22 and September 27, 2023, he exchanged text messages with someone he believed to be the uncle of a 10-year-old boy.  In these messages, Long expressed interest in engaging in sexual activity with the minor child.  On September 27, 2023, Long arrived at a pre-determined location to engage in sex acts with the child and was arrested by law enforcement.  Long also admitted to possessing child pornography on his cellular phone. At sentencing set for February 19, 2027, Long will receive a sentence of at least 10 years and up to life in prison, be placed on supervised release after serving his term of imprisonment for at least five years and up to life, could be fined up to $250,000, and will be required to forfeit to the government the property he used to commit the offenses. In addition, Long will have to register as a sex offender. A defendant’s sentence is imposed by a judge based on the particular statutes the defendant is convicted of violating, the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines, and other factors. First Assistant United States Attorney Sarcone said: “My Office will always prioritize the investigation and prosecution of individuals who commit or try to commit sex crimes against children. I thank the FBI, the New York State Police, and the Colonie Police Department for their diligent investigation.” “Mr. Long admitted to making plans to engage in sex acts with a child he believed was 10-year-old,” said Craig Tremaroli, Special Agent in Charge of the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s Albany Field Office. “Now, his only plans for at least the next decade will include sitting behind bars in federal prison. The FBI’s Child Exploitation and Human Trafficking Task Force will continue to work around the clock to aggressively investigate child predators who seek to harm our most vulnerable and ensure they end up in prison.” This case is being investigated by the FBI and its Child Exploitation Task Force, which includes members of federal, state, and local law enforcement agencies, including the New York State Police and Colonie Police Department.  Assistant United States Attorney A.J. Vickey is prosecuting the case as part of Project Safe Childhood. Project Safe Childhood is a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse. Led by the U.S. Attorneys' Offices and the Criminal Division's Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section (CEOS), Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state and local resources to better locate, apprehend and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the Internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. title: Survey on the Access to Finance of Enterprises: lending conditions tightened
body:
Survey on the Access to Finance of Enterprises: lending conditions tightened Skip to: Skip to navigation Skip to content Skip to footer EN Български Čeština Dansk Deutsch Eλληνικά English Español Eesti keel Suomi Français Gaeilge Hrvatski Magyar Italiano Lietuvių Latviešu Malti Nederlands Polski Português Română Slovenčina Slovenščina Svenska Menu Search Menu ANYTIME PAST MONTH PAST YEAR Search Options Image Preview Sort by ANYTIME PAST MONTH PAST YEAR Suggestions Home Media Explainers Research & Publications Statistics Monetary Policy The €uro Payments & Markets Careers Suggestions Sort by Relevance Date PRESS RELEASE Survey on the Access to Finance of Enterprises: lending conditions tightened 26 October 2026 Firms reported a further net tightening of bank loan interest rates and other loan conditions related to price and non-price factors. Bank loan availability declined by more than financing needs, widening the financing gap. In this survey round the sample composition changed substantially, with first-time respondents accounting for the majority of the sample. This makes it more challenging to interpret the responses to the numerical questions – such as those on expectations for selling prices, input costs and inflation – at this stage. In the most recent round of the Survey on the Access to Finance of Enterprises (SAFE) in the euro area, covering the third quarter of 2026, euro area firms widely reported a further net increase in interest rates on bank loans (net 46%, compared with 42% in the previous quarter). Large firms reported increases more often (net 55%, up from 41%) than small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) (net 38%, down from 43%). At the same time, a net 27% of firms (down from 31% in the previous quarter) reported increases in other financing costs (i.e. charges, fees and commissions) and in collateral requirements (net 14%, up from 10%) (Chart 1). In this survey round, firms reported that the availability of bank loans had declined by more than their needs. Firms reported a decrease in the availability of bank loans in the third quarter of 2026 (-5%, compared with a net -1% in the second quarter of 2026), with both SMEs (net -5%, compared with -4%) and large firms (net -6%, down from 4%) reporting lower availability. At the same time, a net 2% of firms reported a decrease in their bank loan needs, while a net 2% reported an increase in the previous quarter. Developments in needs differed by firm size: SMEs reported broadly unchanged needs (net 1%, compared with 2%), while large firms reported a decrease (net -6%, down from 3%). As a result, the bank loan financing gap indicator, which captures the difference between changes in the need for and the availability of bank loans, was positive (net 2%, compared with 3% in the previous quarter) (Chart 2). Looking ahead, more firms expect the availability of external financing to decrease over the next three months. Firms continued to perceive the general economic outlook as the main factor constraining the availability of external financing (net 31%, compared with 29% in the previous survey round), with large firms now more pessimistic than SMEs (net 35% and 29%, respectively). In this survey round, a net 9% of firms indicated that their firm-specific outlook, in terms of sales and profits, had a negative impact on the availability of external financing (after 10% in the previous survey round), while the impact of their capital position and creditworthiness remained positive. The substantial change in the sample composition in this survey round, with first-time respondents accounting for the majority of the sample, makes it challenging to interpret the responses to the numerical questions at this stage. The increase in selling price expectations was contained among firms that took part in both this round and the previous one, whereas selling price expectations rose significantly in the full sample (Chart 3). Similarly, firms’ median inflation expectations remained broadly unchanged among firms that took part in both the current and previous survey rounds, whereas they rose significantly in the full sample (Chart 4). The risk assessment for firms’ five-year-ahead inflation outlook was broadly unchanged. The report published today presents the main results of the 40th round of the SAFE for the euro area. The survey was conducted between 26 August and 2 October 2026. In this survey round, around half of the firms were asked about changes in the period between July and September 2026. The remainder were asked about changes in the period between April and September 2026. Additionally, firms reported their expectations for euro area inflation, selling prices and other costs. The sample comprised 12,822 enterprises in the euro area, of which 11,917 (93%) had fewer than 250 employees. For media queries, please contact: William Lelieveldt , tel.: +49 170 227 9090. Notes The report on this round of the SAFE, together with the questionnaire and methodological information , is available on the ECB’s website . Detailed data series for the individual euro area countries and aggregate euro area results are available in the ECB Data Portal . Chart 1 Changes in the terms and conditions of bank financing for euro area firms (net percentages of respondents) Base: Firms that had applied for bank loans (including subsidised bank loans), credit lines, or bank or credit card overdrafts. The figures refer to rounds 33 to 40 of the survey (October-December 2024 to July-September 2026). Notes: Net percentages are the difference between the percentage of firms that reported an increase for a given factor and the percentage that reported a decrease. The data included in the chart refer to Question 10 of the survey. Chart 2 Changes in euro area firms’ financing needs and the availability of bank loans (net percentages of respondents) Base: Firms for which the instrument in question is relevant (i.e. they have used it or have considered using it). Respondents who replied “not applicable” or “don’t know” were excluded. The figures refer to rounds 33 to 40 of the survey (October-December 2024 to July-September 2026). Notes: The financing gap indicator combines both financing needs and the availability of bank loans at firm level. The indicator of the perceived change in the financing gap takes a value of 1 (-1) if the need increases (decreases) and availability decreases (increases). If firms perceive only a one-sided increase (decrease) in the financing gap, the variable is assigned a value of 0.5 (-0.5). A positive value for the indicator points to a widening of the financing gap. Values are multiplied by 100 to obtain weighted net balances in percentages. The data included in the chart refer to Question 5 and Question 9 of the survey. Chart 3 Expectations for selling prices, wages, input costs and employees one year ahead (percentage changes over the next 12 months) Base: All firms. The figures refer to rounds 30 to 40 (March 2024 to September 2026) of the survey, with firms’ replies collected in the last month of the respective survey waves. Notes: Mean and median euro area firm expectations of changes in selling prices, wages of current employees, non-labour input costs and number of employees for the next 12 months, along with interquartile ranges, using survey weights. Yellow squares denote the mean expectations of firms interviewed in both the Q2 and Q3 waves of 2026. The statistics are computed after trimming the data at the country-specific 1st and 99th percentiles. The data included in the chart refer to Question 34 of the survey. Chart 4 Firms’ median expectations for euro area inflation at different horizons (annual percentages) Base: All firms. The figures refer to rounds 31 to 40 (June 2024 to September 2026) of the survey, with firms’ replies collected in the last month of the respective survey waves. Notes: Survey-weighted median, mode and interquartile ranges of firms’ expectations for euro area inflation in one year, three years and five years. Quantiles are computed by linear interpolation of the mid-distribution function. Yellow diamonds denote the median expectations of firms interviewed in both the Q2 and Q3 waves of 2026. The statistics are computed after trimming the data at the country-specific 1st and 99th percentiles. The data included in the chart refer to Question 31 of the survey. title: Frank Elderson: Taking action for nature – investing in economic resilience and prosperity
body:
Taking action for nature – investing in economic resilience and prosperity Skip to: Skip to navigation Skip to content Skip to footer EN Български Čeština Dansk Deutsch Eλληνικά English Español Eesti keel Suomi Français Gaeilge Hrvatski Magyar Italiano Lietuvių Latviešu Malti Nederlands Polski Português Română Slovenčina Slovenščina Svenska Menu Search Menu ANYTIME PAST MONTH PAST YEAR Search Options Image Preview Sort by ANYTIME PAST MONTH PAST YEAR Suggestions Home Media Explainers Research & Publications Statistics Monetary Policy The €uro Payments & Markets Careers Suggestions Sort by Relevance Date Frank Elderson Member of the ECB's Executive Board SPEECH Taking action for nature – investing in economic resilience and prosperity Keynote speech by Frank Elderson, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB and Vice-Chair of the Supervisory Board of the ECB, at COP17 Finance and Biodiversity Day Yerewan, 26 October 2026 It is a pleasure to open the Finance and Biodiversity Day at COP17. The theme of this COP is “Taking Action for Nature’’. We have talked about the need for action for long enough. Now we need to act. Four years ago, the international community adopted the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, setting out a pathway to living in harmony with nature by 2050. The destination is set. The path is clear. But progress has remained limited. And nature has not stood still. It has continued to deteriorate. So we need to accelerate. Tangible progress requires a shift from targets to implementation, from awareness to engagement, from ambition to investment. COP17 must help us accelerate the journey. And finance has a central role to play. That should not come as a surprise: without investment, there can be no transition. But we need to get the economics right. Protecting and restoring nature is not simply spending. It is investment: investment in the natural capital on which our economies depend, investment in resilience, and investment in our future prosperity. That is why Finance and Biodiversity Day matters. When ecosystems falter, the economy is at risk Let me start with a fundamental question: why is nature so important to the economy? We tend to think of roads, bridges and electricity grids as critical assets that serve as the foundation of a modern economy. But there is another kind of infrastructure that we often take for granted: natural capital. Nature provides services without which large parts of our economies could not function. Water keeps our factories and farms running, healthy soils sustain our food systems, forests and wetlands regulate droughts and floods, oceans absorb heat and carbon. The World Bank estimates that as much as half of the world’s GDP relies on biodiversity, natural capital and ecosystem services. [ 1 ] Our own analysis shows that 72% of companies in the euro area depend on at least one ecosystem service. And 75% of euro area corporate lending goes to companies that are highly dependent on at least one ecosystem service. [ 2 ] The message is clear: nature is not peripheral to economic activity. It is fundamental to it. But even as we speak, the foundations of our economies are being depleted at an alarming rate. [ 3 ] When ecosystems deteriorate, firms face higher costs, lower productivity and supply chain disruptions. For far too long, we have treated nature as though it were free and inexhaustible. It is neither. We have mistaken the depletion of natural capital for economic prosperity. We counted the production. We counted the income. But we rarely – if ever – counted the soils depleted, the water systems stressed, the forests weakened or the ecosystems lost in producing it. In economic terms, we have been consuming our capital and calling it income. Nature is already presenting us with the bill. Depleted natural capital is already disrupting production, damaging supply chains and increasing costs. The consequences are already spreading from ecosystems to firms, from firms to balance sheets and from balance sheets into the financial system. This is not a future tragedy on the horizon. It is an economic reality unfolding around us. That is why taking action for nature is not only an environmental imperative. It is an economic and financial necessity because our future prosperity directly depends on it. The natural currency underwriting economic activity: water Water is perhaps the clearest example of what happens when we fail to account for natural capital. For too long, we have allowed our economies to function as though reliable supplies of clean water were an unlimited production input. But an economy cannot negotiate with an empty river, a depleted aquifer or a failed ecosystem. When we withdraw water faster than it can be replenished, we are not creating prosperity. We are fooling ourselves and failing future generations by consuming the capital on which future prosperity depends. Think about this summer’s heat-exacerbated drought conditions throughout Europe: major rivers, like the Rhine, Loire, Po and Danube, reached exceptionally low levels, forcing, among other things, the shutdown of critical nuclear power plants, while also negatively affecting hydropower and disrupting supply chains. [ 4 ] Drought also contributed to the severity of wildfires. These are not glimpses of a distant risk. They are stark signs of ecosystems already being pushed beyond their limits, with consequences that are already being felt by people and the economy. Unfortunately, our analysis suggests that the potential consequences could be much larger. Research involving the ECB, the London School of Economics and Oxford University has found that a 1-in-100-year drought event could put up to 24% of euro area economic output at risk. [ 5 ] Clearly, too little water is only half of the story. Too much water can be equally problematic. Nearly 12% of economic output in the euro area faces risks from insufficient flood protection. [ 6 ] The recent catastrophic events in Nepal and Bangkok are a stark reminder of the devastating human consequences alongside the destruction of infrastructure and economic assets. And there is a third dimension to consider: polluted water. Take PFAS, for instance. Known as “forever chemicals”, these pollutants are in a wide range of everyday products from textiles and cookware to batteries and food packaging. As the name suggests, they last an extraordinarily long time – and when they leach into the environment, they can be extremely damaging for people’s health and for entire ecosystems, all of which also comes at substantial economic cost. The European Commission estimates that, if current levels of PFAS pollution in Europe continue until 2050, the cost to society could reach €440 billion over that period. Treating polluted water alone could cost more than €1 trillion. [ 7 ] The economic challenge comes from water in all its dimensions: too little, too much, too hot, too dirty. And the effects differ across regions and sectors: agriculture here, manufacturing there and energy production somewhere else. When sufficiently widespread or persistent, the impacts can ultimately affect growth and inflation. Nature: our first line of defence against the climate crisis But the example of water also reveals something else: climate and nature cannot be separated. Healthy ecosystems act as our first line of defence against global heating and related extreme weather events. Europe is the fastest-warming continent. Temperatures have been rising by approximately 0.56 degrees Celsius per decade since the mid-1990s, more than double the global average. This summer again brought record temperatures, following on from 2025 which was the third-warmest year on record, and 2024, the warmest ever – so far. The interplay between temperature, the water cycle and soil quality illustrates why the climate and nature crises should be treated as a nexus. And perhaps nowhere is this more evident than in the ocean. The ocean is one of our planet’s greatest shock absorbers. It has absorbed around 90% of the excess heat from global warming and around 30% of global carbon dioxide emissions. [ 8 ] That is an extraordinary capacity. But extraordinary does not mean unlimited. Even the strongest buffer has its limits. And those limits are no longer theoretical; we are already breaching them. Seven of the nine planetary boundaries have already been transgressed. We are moving increasingly outside the safe operating space on which our economies and societies depend. [ 9 ] In other words, we are consuming the buffers that protect us from economic disruption and climate shocks at precisely the moment when those shocks are intensifying. Nature – an investment in economic resilience and prosperity Recognising nature as economic infrastructure has another important implication. If degrading nature can weaken our economies, preserving and restoring it can strengthen them. This matters particularly today, when maintaining prosperity, resilience and economic security has taken centre stage in the policy debate. Protecting nature is often framed as if it comes at the expense of competitiveness. However, that frames the problem backwards. As we seek to strengthen prosperity and economic security, nature should be seen as part of the solution rather than as part of a separate, often neglected, environmental agenda. Economic security depends on ecological security. Secure water supplies, resilient food systems, functioning ecosystems and reliable energy systems are strategic assets that reduce vulnerability to future disruptions. We should therefore stop treating investment in nature as a competing claim on prosperity and economic resilience. [ 10 ] It is investment in the productive capacity that makes lasting prosperity possible. There can simply be no lasting prosperity on a collapsing natural foundation. We cannot impoverish nature and expect our economies to flourish. Therefore, preserving and restoring nature is not simply an expenditure. It is an investment. We can invest in preserving and restoring natural capital now. Or we can pay increasingly through disrupted production, adaptation, reconstruction and lost economic capacity later. Nature will impose the adjustment regardless. The question is whether we manage that adjustment, or allow it to be imposed on us. From awareness to action So what does this mean for central banks and banking supervisors? Nature-related risks are global and systemic. They do not stop at borders, and no single jurisdiction can address them alone, which makes international cooperation more indispensable than ever. The current geopolitical fragmentation puts global cooperation at great risk. Encouragingly, the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) shows that international cooperation is alive and can deliver. Bringing together 152 central banks and supervisors across more than 95 countries, alongside 24 observers, the NGFS has over time produced several reports that have helped us to develop common methodologies on risk assessment frameworks, supervision and legal risks. [ 11 ] A recently released compendium of good practices [ 12 ] covers 35 examples of how members assess the physical and transition risk impact of nature-related risks, together with six detailed case studies. In other words, the work of the NGFS has helped lay the groundwork for many of the central banks and supervisors now taking action to account for nature-related risks in their core activities. But the NGFS cannot do this alone. Nature-related financial risks need to remain firmly on the international financial agenda, including at the Basel Committee, the Financial Stability Board and the IMF. At the ECB, this shift from awareness to action is already well advanced. Because nature degradation can affect price stability, financial stability and the safety and soundness of banks, nature-related risks are increasingly part of the bread and butter of our work. In banking supervision, we expect banks to identify and manage not only material climate risks, but also nature-related risks, as part of ensuring banks remain safe and sound. [ 13 ] And our recently updated compendium of good practices shows that banks are increasingly doing just that, with around one-third of the practices relating specifically to nature. [ 14 ] Take price stability, for example. We have found that increases in food prices following extreme heatwaves and droughts are an upside risk to price stability. [ 15 ] Nature risks have therefore featured explicitly in our monetary policy assessment and communication in recent quarters. [ 16 ] Nature is not becoming a feature of central banking because central banks are becoming environmental policymakers. Quite the contrary: we are – and will remain – climate and nature policy takers. Nature is becoming a feature of central banking because the consequences of its degradation are affecting our mandate. Conclusion Let me conclude. Four years have passed since Kunming-Montreal. Nature has not waited. We have developed frameworks, methodologies and tools. But while our understanding improved, the underlying ecological crisis has continued to deepen. Today, 75% of land ecosystems and 66% of ocean ecosystems have been damaged, degraded or modified. Humanity is consuming natural resources around 1.7 times faster than ecosystems can regenerate them. The challenge is no longer simply getting to the destination. It is getting there fast enough before the road towards it disappears. Doing so will require investment at unprecedented scale. Protecting and restoring the natural infrastructure on which economic activity depends will require mobilising substantially greater private capital flows towards nature-positive investments, alongside public finance. [ 17 ] But the longer we delay restoring natural capital, the more costly and difficult restoration becomes. And that brings me back to the purpose of today’s event. I would like to leave you with three key questions that I hope will reverberate throughout this Finance and Biodiversity Day. First, how can we mobilise public and private finance at the scale needed to turn the Kunming-Montreal goals into reality? Second, how can governments, financial institutions, international organisations and other stakeholders work together to help turn nature-positive opportunities that are not yet bankable into investments that can attract capital? And third, how can policy, investment and partnerships help to mobilise finance for projects that generate public goods without direct revenue flows? Kunming-Montreal set the destination. COP17 must now accelerate the journey. Turning awareness into action. Turning targets into tangible results. Turning ambition into investment. Because nature is not waiting. Neither can finance. World Bank (2025), Mainstreaming Nature into World Bank Macroeconomic Models: Overview Report , Washington, D.C. Boldrini, S. et al. (2023), “ Living in a world of disappearing nature: physical risk and the implications for financial stability ”, Occasional Paper Series , No 333, ECB. Recently, the Deutsche Bundesbank published a study that shows the German banking sector is particularly highly dependent on ecosystem services linked to water . 75% of land surface ecosystems and 66% of ocean ecosystems have been damaged, degraded or modified. Around 80% of arable land worldwide is affected by soil erosion, salinisation and biodiversity loss. These pressures are projected to reduce global food productivity by 12% by 2040, increasing food prices by up to 30%. We are running an ecological deficit by using natural resources 1.7 times faster than ecosystems can regenerate them. A landmark report by the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform , published this year and approved by more than 150 member governments, warns that biodiversity loss is among the most serious threats to businesses. The exceptionally low water levels of the Rhine this summer, the lowest since records began in 1880, have not only disrupted transport and industrial production. They could also reduce Germany's economic recovery by up to 0.2 percentage points of GDP in the third quarter. See Ceglar, A. et al., Nature at risk: Implications for the euro area economy and financial stability , Occasional Paper Series , No 380, ECB. See Ceglar, A. et al., ibid. See the European Commission’s web page on PFAS pollution . See the United Nations web page The ocean – the world’s greatest ally against climate change . See the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research’s web page on Planetary Boundaries – defining a safe operating space for humanity . For example, UNEP estimates that every dollar invested in integrated climate change and air pollution action generates around $15 in economic benefits. This would boost global GDP by 2.8% by 2035 and 4.5% by 2050. Against this, implementation costs are expected to amount to around 0.7% of global GDP in the coming decade. See NGFS (2023), Nature-related Financial Risks: a Conceptual Framework to guide Action by Central Banks and Supervisors ; and NGFS (2026), NGFS 2026 Nature Package . NGFS (2026), Water scarcity as a nature-related financial risk: Legal aspects . NGFS, 2026, Nature-related risks: a Compendium of Implementation Practices to guide Action by Central Banks and Supervisors . Today, more than 90% of the banks supervised by the ECB consider themselves to be materially exposed to climate and nature risks, and all have put in place the foundational frameworks needed to identify, assess and manage these risks. While banks have made substantial progress on climate risk, nature-related risks remain considerably less mature. For example, two-thirds of banks do not systematically link their materiality assessment on nature-related risks to a risk management response, and only a few have defined nature-related key risk indicators. Where such indicators exist, they are often used solely for monitoring, with no limits or thresholds to trigger management action Elderson, F. See, e.g. ECB (2026) Combined monetary policy decisions and statement , 23 July. UNEP's State of Finance for Nature 2026 estimates that annual investment in nature-based solutions needs to reach $571 billion by 2030, compared with approximately $220 billion in 2023. That means investment must increase by more than 2.5 times. title: Treasury Issues Proposed Rule to Implement Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security Act
body: October 22, 2026 WASHINGTON– The U.S. Department of the Treasury (Treasury) today issued a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) to propose updates to the Outbound Investment Security Program (OISP) based on direction from Congress in the Comprehensive Outbound Investment Security (COINS) Act, passed as part of the Fiscal Year 2026 National Defense Authorization Act.  The COINS Act codifies the U.S. Government’s approach to regulating certain outbound investments by U.S. persons and builds upon Treasury’s existing OISP. In passing the COINS Act, Congress made clear that restricting certain U.S. outbound investments into dual-use strategic technologies that benefit a foreign adversary’s military modernization efforts, surveillance states, and human rights abuses is necessary to prevent harm to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. President Trump is committed to protecting our national security and the implementation of the COINS Act is consistent with maintaining a strong, open investment environment that benefits our economy and supports our national security interests. The COINS Act directs the Secretary of the Treasury (the Secretary) to issue regulations that (1) require United States persons to provide notification to Treasury regarding certain transactions involving covered foreign persons that are engaged in notifiable technologies, and (2) prohibit United States persons from engaging in certain other transactions involving covered foreign persons that are engaged in prohibited technologies.  The COINS Act authorizes the Secretary to prescribe regulations with technical parameters for “prohibited technology” and “notifiable technology” in five technology sectors: semiconductor technologies and microelectronics; artificial intelligence systems; quantum information technologies; high-performance computing and supercomputing; and hypersonic systems.  The COINS Act also authorizes the Secretary—in consultation with the appropriate congressional committees and subject to notice and comment rulemaking—to add and define technologies beyond those specifically listed in the law that enable the military, intelligence, surveillance, or cyber-enabled capabilities of a country of concern.  Accordingly, the Secretary has added biotechnology to the proposed regulations. “Under President Trump’s leadership, we are committed to putting America’s national security first,” said Secretary Scott Bessent .  “The proposed regulations would strengthen the existing Outbound Investment Security Program to prevent our adversaries from using U.S. investment to develop critical technologies that threaten U.S. national security.  This important step also helps promote our commitment to an open investment environment by providing clarity to U.S. and foreign investors as well as an opportunity for them to provide feedback on the proposed regulations.” “The proposed regulations are designed to address risks that can arise when foreign adversaries try to benefit from U.S. investment in key technology sectors,” said Assistant Secretary of the Treasury for Investment Security Christopher Pilkerton.  Pilkerton added, “It will enhance the Outbound Investment Security Program and our efforts to protect U.S. national security.” The NPRM issued today provides details on key concepts and aspects of the program’s proposed implementation, including: Requirements applicable to a U.S. person (including any controlled foreign entities); Categories of covered national security transactions; Definitions; The scope of covered foreign persons; Excepted transactions; Technical specifications to inform the scope of covered national security transactions based on certain technologies and products in the areas of semiconductor technology and microelectronics, quantum information technologies, super intelligence systems, hypersonic systems, high-performance computing and supercomputing, and biotechnology; Information that a U.S. person is required to provide to Treasury as part of a notification; The process of requesting non-binding feedback and submitting confidential information; The knowledge standard and expectations for a U.S. person to conduct a reasonable and diligent inquiry prior to undertaking a transaction; and Conduct that would be treated as a violation of the proposed rule and applicable penalties for such conduct. Treasury invites comments from a wide range of stakeholders on all aspects of the NPRM including feedback on the scope of a covered national security transaction, definitions of key terms, the notification requirements, and the penalty and enforcement processes for violations, among other aspects.  Treasury will carefully consider this input before issuing the final implementing regulations. Written comments may be submitted by the deadline in the official NPRM, available at https://www.regulations.gov .  The NPRM will be followed at a later date by final implementing regulations, which will set an effective date for the program. The NPRM, fact sheet, and additional information are available at: https://home.treasury.gov/policy-issues/international/outbound-investment-program .

title: The Trump Administration is Making Homeownership More Affordable
body: October 22, 2026 Proposed Rules Implement the ROAD to Housing Act and Support Affordable Homeownership in America WASHINGTON — Today, the U.S. Department of the Treasury issued proposed regulations to make homeownership more affordable for hardworking Americans. The proposed regulations implement Section 1001 of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act (ROAD to Housing Act), which restricts large institutional investors from purchasing single-family homes, codifying key requirements of President Trump’s Executive Order 14376 , Stopping Wall Street from Competing with Main Street Homebuyers . “Under President Trump, this Administration continues to restore the path to affordable homeownership for millions of young and working families,” said Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent . “Treasury is working to ensure American families and workers have a fair shot at purchasing homes in their communities by increasing housing supply and limiting large institutional investors’ role in the market, while supporting a strong, stable housing market and avoiding unnecessary disruption.” RESTORING THE AMERICAN DREAM OF HOMEOWNERSHIP Beginning on January 7, 2027, a large institutional investor generally may not purchase, or enter into a contract to purchase, a single-family home unless the purchase qualifies as an “excepted purchase” under the ROAD to Housing Act. The ROAD to Housing Act defines a large institutional investor by reference to, among other things, whether an entity is engaged in the business of investing in, owning, renting, managing, or holding single-family homes and has direct or indirect investment control over at least 350 such homes. The ROAD to Housing Act permits several categories of excepted purchases, including purchases made pursuant to build-to-rent programs, renovate-to-rent programs, homeownership programs, and programs to boost homeownership. Today’s NPRM sets forth Treasury’s proposed framework to: Establish standards for purchases made pursuant to build-to-rent programs that promote continued investment in new housing; Provide a safe harbor for purchases made pursuant to renovate-to-rent programs that bring neglected homes back into the housing supply and up to code; Clarify the requirements for homeownership programs and programs to boost homeownership, including providing safe harbors for large institutional investors that provide meaningful financial support towards their renters’ purchase of a home; Clarify that an entity is engaged “in the business of” investing in , owning, renting, managing, or holding single-family homes when it does so for the purpose of receiving income or financial gain, and not incidentally to a different business; Define when an entity may qualify as a passive investor in another entity that owns a home because it does not share directors or officers with the other entity and does not have a property control right over the underlying homes; Clarify certain purchases involving debts previously contracted, loss mitigation, and transfers between large institutional investors that protect the liquidity of the housing market; and Clarify the calculation of the maximum civil penalty where a single prohibited purchase involves more than one large institutional investor. The proposed rule would provide non-exclusive safe harbors for several statutory requirements. These include standards for determining whether a home has been substantially rehabilitated under a renovate-to-rent program, whether a renter has received meaningful financial support under certain homeownership programs, and whether a renter has received a right of first refusal and 30-day first-look period. Treasury’s proposed approach recognizes that housing-market participants use a variety of ownership, investment, construction, servicing, and property-management structures and seeks to provide clarity without unnecessary disruption to housing supply, homebuilding, rehabilitation activity, or capital formation. Members of the public should submit comments in response to the NPRM within 30 days after publication in the Federal Register. The proposed regulations are available here . ###

title: October 22, 2026 - FDA Launches New Program to Advance Neuroscience Medical Product Development
body: FDA News Release FDA Launches New Program to Advance Neuroscience Medical Product Development Neuroscience Advancement and Innovation Nexus to coordinate agency action on brain and nervous system conditions, with inaugural focus on Alzheimer's prevention For Immediate Release: October 22, 2026 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today announced the launch of the Neuroscience Advancement and Innovation Nexus (NAIN) , a new agency program aligned with the Trump Administration’s efforts to accelerate medical innovation and deliver breakthrough treatments. NAIN is designed to advance the science, tools, and regulatory approaches needed to support the development of medical products for conditions affecting the brain and nervous system. NAIN’s inaugural initiative, the Alzheimer's Prevention Accelerator , will focus on advancing medical products that help delay or prevent Alzheimer's disease. Both efforts support the National Alzheimer’s Project Act (NAPA), the federal government's comprehensive roadmap for coordinated action on Alzheimer's and related dementias. "The launch of NAIN reflects FDA's commitment — in support of the Trump Administration’s drive to transform health care innovation — to making sure our regulatory science and cross-center collaboration keep pace with the rapid advances happening in neuroscience," said Acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas, J.D. "Through NAIN and the Alzheimer's Prevention Accelerator, we are bringing the full breadth of FDA's expertise to bear on one of the most urgent public health challenges of our time.” Developing medical products for neuroscience indications is associated with complex scientific and clinical challenges, including limited understanding of underlying biology, variable disease presentation, and difficulties in demonstrating meaningful clinical benefit, particularly for conditions that develop over many years. Advances in biomarkers, digital health technologies, and other medical product development tools, however, offer important opportunities to address these challenges. NAIN will bring together scientific and regulatory expertise from the FDA's Center for Drug Evaluation and Research, Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research, and Center for Devices and Radiological Health to address scientific and regulatory questions that benefit from coordinated consideration across drugs, biologics, and devices. NAIN will encompass conditions that affect the brain and nervous system broadly, including neurologic and psychiatric disorders, substance use disorders, and pain. NAIN will also support robust engagement with patients, industry, academia and other stakeholders to advance these efforts. As its first initiative, NAIN is launching the Alzheimer's Prevention Accelerator . This inaugural initiative will draw on perspectives from across the FDA and engage patients and caregivers, researchers, industry, public-private partnerships and other government agencies. The initiative will explore innovative approaches to advancing clinical trials for Alzheimer’s disease prevention and early-intervention drug development with emphasis on trial populations, stage-appropriate endpoints, and evidentiary approaches for demonstrating prevention or delay of cognitive decline due to Alzheimer’s disease. The FDA has long been committed to supporting the development of safe and effective medical products that address diseases and conditions of the brain and nervous system. Through NAIN and the Alzheimer's Prevention Accelerator, the agency is taking a proactive, coordinated approach to accelerating progress, bringing together its scientific and regulatory expertise, engaging the broader research and development community, and working in concert with federal partners to meet the scale of this public health challenge.
